extracted.intended_audience: general readers, reformers, policymakers, and students of political economy interested in the causes of poverty and land reform
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and evaluates the criteria Henry George uses to judge proposed remedies for poverty and social distress, especially in relation to land ownership and rent. The chapter groups and reviews commonly advocated measures and tests them against the principle that land monopoly captures gains from productive progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater economy in government
rubrics_metrics.description: I.—From Greater Economy in Government. (Reduction in public expenditures and taxation is commonly proposed as a remedy for poverty.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reduction in taxation or public expenditure is equivalent to an increase in net productive power; such gains will, like gains from improved arts or machinery, be absorbed as increased land rent while land remains monopolized. Temporary improvements might follow a sudden cut in expenses, but ultimately English (or local) landowners will reap the benefit and the condition of wage-earners will not be permanently improved. Examples/analogy: hypothetical repudiation of English debt, disestablishment, disbanding military/navy—would add to net produce but increase rent; comparison to effects of railroads and machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diffusion of education and improved habits of industry and thrift
rubrics_metrics.description: II.—From the Diffusion of Education and Improved Habits of Industry and Thrift. (Widely held belief that poverty stems from lack of industry, frugality, intelligence.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned as a commonly advocated remedy. Implied critique (developed elsewhere in the work): while education and thrift are desirable, they cannot extirpate poverty if land is monopolized because increased productive power without changing land tenure will be captured as rent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations of workmen for the advance of wages
rubrics_metrics.description: III.—From Combinations of Workmen for the Advance of Wages. (Organizing labor to raise wages is proposed as a remedy.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among the principal classes of proposed remedies to be reviewed. Treated as one of several measures whose ultimate efficacy must be judged by whether it prevents rent from absorbing gains; specifics are to be evaluated against the central principle of land monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-operation of labor and capital
rubrics_metrics.description: IV.—From the Co-operation of Labor and Capital. (The idea that labor and capital working together will raise wages and relieve poverty.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as a commonly advocated approach. Its sufficiency is questioned implicitly: cooperation that increases productive power without altering land ownership will tend to increase land value/rent rather than permanently raise wages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governmental direction and interference
rubrics_metrics.description: V.—From Governmental Direction and Interference. (Direct government action or control proposed to remedy social distress.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counted among the six main classes of remedies. Any governmental measure that increases net production or transfers wealth without addressing land monopoly risks having its benefits appropriated as rent; the chapter urges evaluating such measures for whether they alter land tenure or the incidence of rent.

rubrics_metrics.name: More general distribution of land
rubrics_metrics.description: VI.—From a More General Distribution of Land. (Wider distribution of land-ownership proposed as a remedy.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as one of the principal categories of proposed remedies. This category is directly relevant to the central thesis: distribution or democratization of access to land addresses the root cause (land monopoly) and therefore stands apart from other measures that merely increase productive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increases in productive power without altering land tenure benefit landlords, not labor
rubrics_metrics.description: A reduction in taxation or any increase in the net produce of a community is equivalent to an increase in productive power and, while increasing aggregate wealth, will be appropriated as increased land rent if land is monopolized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core evaluative principle repeated across examples: improvements from machinery, railroads, discovery, or governmental economy have historically increased rent rather than wages. Examples: railroads, steam and machinery, California placer gold (where free land briefly raised wages until monopolization), Comstock lode (monopolizable resources added to land value), hypothetical English reforms. Use this test when judging remedies: if they merely increase net production without changing land monopoly, they will not permanently help wage-earners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of land monopolization determines wages and distribution of wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not abundance of capital or productiveness of labor that makes wages high or low; but the extent to which the monopolizers of land can, in rent, levy tribute upon the earnings of labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparisons across places and times to evaluate social conditions: new countries with cheap land have higher wages and less pauperism despite lower aggregate wealth; old countries with dear land show deeper poverty amid abundance. Historical examples: medieval England after enclosure, comparative rents and wages across London, New York, San Francisco, England over centuries. Any remedy must be assessed on whether it reduces the landlords' ability to levy rent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary improvements versus long-term capture by land values
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporary and recurring depressions and temporary improvements are intensifications or phases of a general movement; even substantial sudden reforms may produce only temporary improvements because increased land values will eventually swallow gains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a proposed remedy, distinguish between transient effects and durable change: a sudden policy change might yield a short-term rise in wages, but if it leaves land monopoly intact the resulting wealth will be capitalized into land values and the working class will not be permanently bettered. Example: brief post-reform upticks vs eventual speculative advance of land values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies must prevent capture of gains by rent to be effective
rubrics_metrics.description: Any measure that aims to raise the permanent condition of a people must not merely increase net production but must prevent the gains being absorbed by increased rent arising from land monopoly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter frames the true remedy as 'radical and simple' because only measures that alter the relation of land ownership or the incidence of rent can permanently raise wages and relieve poverty. Thus one should evaluate policy proposals by whether they directly address ownership or taxation of land (i.e., remove or neutralize the ability of landowners to appropriate gains).
